$schema-note: Every difference between a v9 frame and the implementation lands in exactly one class. Gate B reads this file and enforces the rules below — the classification is not advisory prose.

classes.MUST-FIX: Clearly violates v9 with no functionality or accessibility reason. Implement the v9 design exactly. BLOCKS its frame until closed. No approval needed to fix — fixing toward v9 is the mandate.
classes.APPROVED-DEVIATION: Existing functionality or accessibility requires something different from v9. DO NOT MODIFY until the owner explicitly approves. Blocks its frame while status is pending.
classes.PRODUCT-DECISION: The v9 HTML specifies a different workflow or different copy, and choosing between them is the owner's call, not an engineering one. DO NOT MODIFY until the owner explicitly approves. Blocks its frame while status is pending.
classes.NOT-BUILT: The surface or its server support does not exist yet. Leave untouched until its assigned migration task runs. Does not block a frame for a defect it cannot have.

deviations.summary: Free-form voice intent routing has no surface in the app since ruling #30 removed VoiceCommandHero

The orb is a voice affordance in NAME (mic icon, hold menu) but not in behaviour: nav-dock.tsx:59 is `onTap={() => router.push(action.href)}` and voice-menu.tsx:87 is `router.push(row.href)`. Ruling #30's stated rationale was 'the dock orb remains the single global voice affordance'. That premise is true of the icon and false of the behaviour, so the ruling was likely made without this being visible.

deviations.summary: A rejected consultation made its visit permanently un-recordable — the root cause of #44
deviations.reason: POST /consultations returns the EXISTING consultation for a visit whatever its status (consultations.ts findUnique on visitId). Once a doctor taps Re-record — which posts /consultations/:id/reject and sets status REJECTED — and then leaves the screen or the app reloads, tapping Record for that patient in the queue re-enters the same REJECTED consultation. deriveStateFromView returns {kind:'REJECTED'} and the consult page router.replace's back to /consult. The doctor taps Record, is bounced to the queue, and the visit can never be recorded again — silently, with no error. Reproduced against the live stack: D2/D3/D4/D5 capture now dead-ends on the queue screen.
deviations.ruling: APPROVED AS MUST-FIX (owner, verbatim): "A REJECTED consultation represents a rejected recording/processing attempt, NOT a permanently unusable visit. POST /consultations for a visit that already has a REJECTED consultation must reuse that existing consultation and reset it to PENDING_REVIEW so the doctor can record again... The rejection itself MUST remain durable in AuditLog via CONSULTATION_REJECTED. Do NOT drop the unique Consultation.visitId constraint. Do NOT create a second consultation record for the same visit as part of this fix. Do NOT remove or weaken the audit trail."
deviations.fixedIn: apps/api/src/routes/consultations.ts — POST /consultations resets a REJECTED consultation in place: status PENDING_REVIEW, and every field that is the rejected ATTEMPT's own output cleared (structuredData, rejectedById, rejectedReason, rawTranscriptEnc, audioUrl, audioStorageKey, audioDurationMs, languageCode, provider, sttLatencyMs, extractionLatencyMs, safetyWarnings). The schema was inspected per the ruling: those are precisely the transient/derived columns of one recording. Patient, Visit, ConsultationEdit and AuditLog are untouched, the unique visitId constraint stands, and no second row is created. A CONSULTATION_REOPENED audit row records the reset. Regression: apps/api/test/consultation-reject-then-rerecord.test.ts covers all eight required proofs. Clearing the transcript and audio key is the safety half — without it the next take would inherit the abandoned recording's dictation.

deviations.summary: Frame 27's "Swap → Azithro 500" — no drug-substitution knowledge base exists
deviations.reason: The frame resolves an allergy conflict by swapping to a NAMED alternative antibiotic, and frame 28 shows the result ('swapped for Amoxicillin · allergy-safe'). Nothing in the app knows that azithromycin is the penicillin-safe substitute: SafetyWarning carries code, message, field and detail — no alternative — and there is no substitution table anywhere in the API. Hardcoding one inside a UI task would be inventing prescribing advice, which is the single thing this product must never do. The conflict rail ships with the frame's full anatomy (red rail, red drug name, one factual line, inline action) and the action is 'Remove', which is the resolution the safety model actually recognises (isResolved: the flagged medicine is no longer prescribed). It says Remove rather than Swap so the doctor is never told the app chose a replacement drug.
deviations.openQuestion: Build drug substitution? It needs a clinical data source, an owner for its correctness, and a decision about liability — the app would be suggesting a specific prescription. Recommend a dedicated task with clinical sign-off, not a migration task.
deviations.reclassified: 2026-09-07 - was NOT-BUILT/open, which read as work still to come. It is not: product rule 6 ('AI must not invent medication substitutions') forbids the swap permanently, and no drug-substitution knowledge base is planned. The card resolves a conflict by REMOVING the drug -- the resolution the safety model actually recognises -- and the button says 'Remove' rather than implying the app chose a replacement. Reclassified so the ledger states a settled decision instead of a pending task.

deviations.summary: The FINDINGS and PROCEDURE prose sections have no extraction fields behind them

deviations.summary: Confirm stays available over an allergy conflict; the dentist decides and the override is audited
deviations.reason: Frame 27 shows 'Confirm & save' disabled while the allergy conflict is unresolved, and the task brief repeats it. That is a CLINICAL POLICY change, not a visual one. Today allergy_conflict is an advisory warning, not a blocking error: the API's own prompt says 'Do NOT remove the prescription — flag it; the doctor decides', and confirming over a live warning is a supported, audited path (confirmedWithWarning -> CONSULTATION_CONFIRMED_WITH_WARNING). Disabling Confirm would remove a doctor's documented authority to prescribe against a flag they have judged — for example a recorded 'rash' that they know to be tolerable. Implemented as today: Confirm is gated by BLOCKING errors only, and the conflict is drawn loudly on the drug.
deviations.openQuestion: Should an unresolved allergy conflict HARD-BLOCK confirm, overriding the doctor? Recommend no — keep the override with its audit trail, since the alternative is a clinician unable to file a record they believe is correct. If yes, the API's warning/blocking classification must change too, so the two layers do not disagree.
deviations.ruling: OWNER RULING: 'KEEP Confirm & Save available during an allergy conflict. Do NOT hard-block confirmation. The current behavior is: OdoVox detects/receives an allergy conflict; OdoVox clearly warns the dentist; dentist reviews the conflict; dentist may remove/change the prescription; dentist may explicitly override the warning if clinically appropriate; the override is recorded in the audit trail. Do NOT invent automatic drug substitutions. Do NOT allow Gemini/LLM output to determine whether an allergy conflict is an absolute contraindication. Any future hard-block policy must come from an explicit clinical safety policy/knowledge layer, not visual matching of the V9 frame.'
deviations.fixedIn: No code change — the ruling confirms the behaviour already shipped, and records WHY it is correct rather than incidental. Confirm is gated by BLOCKING errors only; an allergy conflict is advisory, drawn loudly on the drug itself (red rail, red name, one factual line). Overriding it commits through the existing confirmedWithWarning path and lands in AuditLog as CONSULTATION_CONFIRMED_WITH_WARNING. Frame 27's greyed-out CTA is therefore an APPROVED DEVIATION: matching it would remove a clinician's documented authority on the strength of a visual, which the ruling forbids. Related: #51 stays NOT-BUILT — no automatic substitution is invented, and the conflict action removes the drug rather than choosing a replacement.

deviations.summary: Reception's patient rows carried a medical flag; ruled out — reception queue is not a clinical record
deviations.reason:
Reopened at the owner's instruction. I had closed this as an APPROVED-DEVIATION on my own judgement, which was not mine to make.

WHAT THE V9 FRAME SHOWS (frames 32/33): each row is avatar, name, then a glyph strip of TOOTH NUMBER, SITTING PROGRESS DOTS (filled/current/remaining) and DUES in crit — plus a trailing status dot. It reads as a treatment-progress list.

WHAT THE IMPLEMENTATION SHOWS: avatar, name, then AGE, CHIEF COMPLAINT, the first MEDICAL FLAG in crit (DIABETES, HYPERTENSION) and DUES in crit — plus the trailing status dot. It reads as a patient-identity list. The avatar ring and dot now carry live queue state (#62).

LOST BY MATCHING THE FRAME: the medical flag, which is the only place a receptionist opening a record sees a condition before they act, and the frame has nowhere to put it. Age also goes — the everyday disambiguator between two patients with the same name.

GAINED BY MATCHING THE FRAME: which tooth is being treated and how far through the plan the patient is, without opening the record. For a clinic scanning for 'who is mid-RCT' that is the more useful list.

WHICH KIND OF DECISION: primarily WORKFLOW — who is scanning this list and what for. It has a CLINICAL edge, because dropping the medical flag removes safety information from a receptionist-visible surface. It is not a visual decision; both versions are the same component with different facts in it. It also carries a technical cost: tooth + sitting dots require joining every row to its active plan, the widening deferred in #48.
deviations.ruling: OWNER RULING: 'I am choosing the receptionist/queue workflow over exposing clinical information on the queue card. The receptionist-facing patient/queue card should NOT display medical flags or allergies. #69 established the clinical/privacy boundary. Medical flags are clinically relevant to the dentist, not a general receptionist queue surface. The doctor-facing /consult surface already exposes the relevant allergy information. Do not expose medical conditions simply because they happen to exist in the payload. KEEP: patient identity, operational queue information, dues/billing information, complaint if it is already part of the approved workflow. PREFER tooth / treatment sitting / treatment progress IF the required structured data already exists or is introduced by an already-planned task. DO NOT create speculative clinical data. RECEPTION QUEUE ≠ CLINICAL RECORD.'
deviations.openQuestion: Which list is this? Options: (a) keep as-is — identity + safety, no extra query; (b) match the frame — treatment progress, losing the medical flag and needing the plan join; (c) both, dropping age to make room, still needing the join. I recommend (c) if the join is acceptable, since it keeps the safety flag and gains the clinical progress, but this is your ruling and I am not resolving it.
deviations.fixedIn: The medical-flag chip is removed from the /patients row. What remains is what reception works with: identity (name, age), the live queue state on the avatar ring and trailing dot, the complaint, and dues in crit. The doctor still sees allergies where they act on them — prominently on the in-chair card behind DOCTOR/ADMIN (#69). The privacy regression test now treats /patients as a reception surface, so a future edit cannot quietly put flags back.

deviations.summary: The day river counted cancelled appointments and put the chair marker on the wrong patient
deviations.reason: Frame 13's river is the habit hook — one segment per appointment, lime done, dark in the chair. It was fed `appointments.length` raw, so cancellations and no-shows drew as work still ahead: a doctor with three call-offs saw a day that was fuller than it was. And the chair marker was placed at index `done`, assuming the patient in the chair is always the next one after the finished ones — a walk-in seen between booked slots put the dark segment on somebody else. The caption also mixed sources, taking 'to go' from the live queue rather than the day, and omitted the frame's takings clause entirely.
deviations.fixedIn: apps/web/lib/queue/day-river-view.ts — dayShape() filters CANCELLED/NO_SHOW and locates the chair by patientId against the FILTERED list; dayCaption() builds the frame's line and drops clauses that would read as bad news rather than no news ('0 seen · 0 to go · ₹0 in' at 9am describes a disaster; it is just early). 11 tests.

The day river therefore rendered null (it returns null at zero segments), 'Up next' was always empty and the Schedule screen had nothing in it — in every demo and every screenshot, regardless of what else was going on. deviations.summary: The captured river is shorter than frame 13's, because the harness pins the clock to a past date
deviations.reason: The screenshot harness pins the browser clock to 2026-07-13T09:41 so every capture is deterministic — that is where both panels' 'MON · 13 JUL 9:41' comes from. The SERVER runs on real time, so appointments seeded onto that date are weeks overdue as far as the API is concerned and the NO_SHOW sweep correctly retires the future ones. The capture therefore shows the two completed plus the patient in the chair, and the caption's 'to go' and '₹ in' clauses have nothing to say. That is the app behaving correctly on a past-dated fixture, not a defect: on the real today the seeded day renders in full (verified — 2 COMPLETED, 1 CHECKED_IN, 3 SCHEDULED survive).
deviations.ruling: Self-resolved. Closing it properly means either moving the pinned date forward on every capture run or freezing server time too; both are harness changes with their own risks, and neither belongs in a frame task.

deviations.reason: Frame 41 pairs 'Collect ₹3,000' with a 'Remind' action. deviations.openQuestion: Add a payment-reminder template? It needs the copy drafted and submitted for approval, and a decision about whether payment chasing over WhatsApp is something the product does at all.

deviations.summary: The billing headline drops gross 'Billed' for the frame's OUTSTANDING / PAID pair
deviations.reason: The tab showed three figures — Billed, Paid, Due. Frame 41 shows two: OUTSTANDING in crit and PAID · ALL TIME. Gross billed is the one figure that changes no decision a receptionist is making at that moment, and it remains on every bill row below, so nothing is lost.
deviations.ruling: Self-resolved as presentation: no figure is removed from the screen, only from the headline.

deviations.summary: The billing tab fetched bills twice, from two different endpoints
deviations.reason: Rows came from useBills() and the summary from /patients/:id/billing. Two requests, two snapshots: a payment landing between them left a row and the total above it disagreeing. The ruling forbids a second billing source of truth, and this was one.
deviations.fixedIn: Rows and summary both come from /patients/:id/billing, which now carries the derived description and payment context. One request, one snapshot.

deviations.summary: The full identity block stays on every tab; v9 shows a compact header on 38/40/41
deviations.reason:
Frame 37 gives the patient a large centred identity block. Frames 38, 40 and 41 replace it with a compact strip — small avatar, name, one action — to buy vertical space for the tab's own content. The implementation keeps the full block throughout.

It is a real difference and it costs roughly 150px on three tabs. It is recorded rather than built because the compact header carries a DIFFERENT action per tab (+ Plan on Cases, PDF on Billing, nothing on Teeth), which is four header variants and a per-tab action contract — more than a restyle, and it interacts with the Task 23 case-detail screen that owns some of those actions. Nothing is lost meanwhile: the identity, the flags and the three stats stay visible on every tab, which is more context than the frames give, not less.
deviations.ruling: Self-resolved as layout: no information or action is removed, only repeated.

deviations.summary: Frame 38's "Schedule remaining" — the capability EXISTS; the Cases card does not reach it
deviations.reason:
CORRECTION. This was recorded as NOT-BUILT on the claim that nothing books a plan's outstanding sittings in one action. That claim was wrong, and I did not check hard enough before writing it: POST /appointments/recurring exists, useCreateRecurring() calls it, and the case-detail page already renders a full 'Schedule remaining sittings' control — interval choice (weekly / fortnightly / monthly), a dated preview of every sitting it will create, and a SERIES_UNSCHEDULED error path for slots it cannot place.

So the real gap is navigational, not functional: frame 38's card has no route to a control that is one screen away. Task 23 builds that case-detail screen to the frame and performs its link audit, which is the right place to close this.
deviations.fixedIn: Link audit (Global Constraint 10): every site rendering a plan or procedure name now navigates to case detail — the Overview active-case card, the Teeth tab's tooth panel, the Cases tab's past and secondary plans, the journey's 'Open case', and the PRIMARY active plan's heading, which was the one that did not and is why the control looked missing. 'Schedule remaining sittings' lives on that screen with its interval choice and dated preview; the heading is how frame 38 reaches it. Titles use caseTitle() so the words match the screen they open.

deviations.summary: Journey steps are titled by procedure; v9 titles them by clinical step name
deviations.reason: Frame 38 reads 'Sitting 1 · Access opening', 'Sitting 2 · Cleaning & shaping' — the clinical step each sitting performs. A Sitting has a number and encrypted notes; it has no step-name field, and inventing one per sitting number would be the app asserting a clinical protocol it has no source for (RCT step 2 is not universally 'cleaning & shaping'). Steps are titled by the procedure instead, and the doctor's own note carries the detail where it exists — '28 Jun · extirpation, dressing', which is the same information from an authoritative source.
deviations.ruling: Self-resolved: naming clinical steps from a number would be inventing clinical truth.

deviations.summary: Sitting rows show no per-sitting fee — Sitting has no cost field
deviations.reason: Frame 39's sitting rows read '28 Jun · ₹2,500' — what that individual visit cost. A Sitting carries a number, a visit link, encrypted notes and a completion time; it has no money on it, and bills attach to visits and procedures rather than to sittings. Splitting a procedure's bill evenly across its sittings would invent a per-visit price nobody charged. The row shows its date; the money lives on the FEES tile as a plan total, which IS derived from real bill items.
deviations.openQuestion: Should a sitting carry its own charge? It would need a product decision about whether clinics price per sitting or per procedure — they do both — before any schema change.

deviations.summary: The case screen was titled "Treatment Plan" rather than naming the case
deviations.reason: Every other surface refers to this case as 'RCT · Tooth 36'. Landing on a screen headed 'Treatment Plan' makes a doctor check they opened the right one. The header now carries the case's own name, with the sitting chip beside it.
deviations.fixedIn: caseTitle() builds it from the plan name plus its teeth, appending the tooth only when the name does not already carry it — the same duplication that produced 'RCT · Tooth 36 · Tooth 36' on the Overview card.

deviations.summary: FEES and NEXT read empty in the capture because the fixture has no billed or booked work
deviations.reason: FEES shows ₹0 / 9,000 because no bill item in the seed points at this plan's procedure — the derivation is correct and tested (7 tests), there is simply nothing paid to report. NEXT reads 'Not booked' for the pinned-clock reason already recorded as #66: the harness freezes the browser at 2026-07-13 while the server runs on real time, so an appointment seeded onto that date is in the past as far as the API is concerned. Both are fixture conditions, not defects.
deviations.ruling: Self-resolved as a test-fixture matter, consistent with #66.

deviations.summary: History is a route reached from the overflow menu, not a sixth tab
deviations.reason: The plan allows either, provided no existing tab is removed, and none is. Five tabs already crowd a 370px row — the labels had to lose their padding when 'Overview' truncated — so a sixth would truncate them again. History lives at /patients/[id]/history, reached from the record's overflow menu.
deviations.ruling: Self-resolved: the plan delegates the choice explicitly.

deviations.summary: A recorded allergy has no date — frame 42 shows one ('2019')
deviations.reason: Frame 42 dates the permanent medical fact: 'Penicillin allergy recorded — 2019'. The patient record stores allergies as encrypted free text with no timestamp and no author, so there is no year to show. The entry carries a null date and is pinned under 'ON RECORD' at the end of the timeline rather than being given a fabricated one — a wrong date on a clinical fact is worse than no date, because it invites reasoning about when the patient developed it.
deviations.openQuestion: Should allergies become dated, authored records rather than a free-text column? That is a clinical data-model decision — it would let the timeline show when and by whom — and it needs your ruling before any schema change.

deviations.summary: The seed recorded the same allergy in one place and not the other
deviations.reason: Akhilesh carried medicalFlags ['PENICILLIN_ALLERGY'] but no allergiesEnc. The in-chair card reads flags and the history reads the encrypted field, so the demo asserted the patient was allergic on one screen and silent about it on another. Both now carry it.
deviations.fixedIn: packages/db/prisma/seed.ts sets medicalFlags and allergiesEnc together.

deviations.summary: Re-running the seed failed on the lab case's unique caseNumber
deviations.reason: The new lab-case fixture cleaned up by treatmentPlanId, but the plan is recreated with a fresh id on every run, so the delete never matched the previous run's case and the second seed died on (clinicId, caseNumber). `pnpm db:seed` is the documented way back to a known demo; it has to survive being run twice.
deviations.fixedIn: Deletes by caseNumber. Verified by running the seed twice in a row.

deviations.summary: The visit-record sheet needs FINDINGS and PROCEDURE prose that is not extracted
deviations.reason:
Frame 43 is a read-only record of one visit, and its body is two narrative sections — FINDINGS ('Deep caries distal 36, tenderness on percussion...') and PROCEDURE ('Access opening under LA, four canals located...'). ClinicalExtraction has one free-text field, `notes`, which is where dictated patient advice lands; there is no findings field and no procedure narrative. The rest of the sheet is buildable — audioDurationMs exists, bills and prescriptions are joinable, and Amend has its append-only ConsultationEdit path — but a visit record whose two clinical sections are empty is not the record the frame describes, and generating that prose is exactly what product rule 7 forbids.

Sitting rows on frame 39 therefore do not offer to open it: they render without a chevron rather than as buttons that lead somewhere disappointing.
deviations.openQuestion: Same dependency as #52 — add `findings` and `procedureNarrative` to ClinicalExtraction and the clinical prompt. Recommend scheduling both with extraction work, where the prompt and its tests live, rather than inside a UI task.
deviations.ownerRuling: 2026-09-07 - OWNER RULING, verbatim: 'Build the fixture, defer the fields.' `findings` and `procedureNarrative` are NOT added to ClinicalExtraction and the clinical prompt is NOT changed as part of this UI migration - changing what the AI extracts has its own blast radius and needs its own clinical review. PaperBlock and the visit record render the sections that HAVE data and omit the sections that do not; they never generate prose to fill them (product rule 7). These frames are recorded rather than force-matched.

deviations.summary: CLINICAL: frame 45 LOCKS 'Share Rx PDF' while an allergy conflict is unresolved
deviations.reason:
Frame 45 greys the share button and captions it 'Locked while a conflict is unresolved'. That is a clinical hard block, and product rules 4 and 8 reserve those for you: the dentist is the final clinical decision maker, and a hard-block policy must come from an explicit clinical decision rather than from matching a frame.

You already ruled the equivalent question on the verification card (#53): Confirm stays available over an allergy conflict, the dentist may override, and the override is audited. The consistent answer here is that Share stays available.

But it is NOT obviously the same act, which is why I am not deciding it. Confirming a record files what happened. Sharing a prescription PDF hands the patient a document telling them to take a drug the record says they react to — the artefact leaves the clinic and outlives the conversation. A hard block is more defensible here than on Confirm.

NOT IMPLEMENTED. Share remains available and the conflict is drawn loudly on the drug itself.
deviations.openQuestion: Three options. (a) Consistent with #53: Share stays available, conflict shown loudly, override audited. (b) Hard block per the frame. (c) Middle: Share stays available but requires an explicit acknowledgement that is recorded, the way confirmedWithWarning already works. I recommend (c) — it keeps the dentist deciding while making the decision auditable on a document that leaves the building. Either (b) or (c) is a clinical-policy decision and needs your ruling.
deviations.ownerRuling: 2026-09-07 - OWNER RULING, verbatim: 'Share stays available, log it.' Share Rx PDF is NOT locked by an unresolved allergy conflict. This is consistent with ruling #53 on the verification card: an allergy warning is advisory, the dentist is the final clinical decision maker, and the override is audited. Sharing over an unresolved conflict is recorded as a share-with-warning audit event. Frame 45's greyed button and its 'Locked while a conflict is unresolved' caption are therefore NOT implemented; the conflict rail still renders prominently above the share control.
deviations.resolution: Share control stays enabled. The conflict rail renders above it. Taking Share while a conflict is open emits an audited share-with-warning event, mirroring CONSULTATION_CONFIRMED_WITH_WARNING.

deviations.summary: Frame 45's 'Swap' chip is an automatic drug substitution — forbidden by rule 6
deviations.reason: The conflict row in frame 45 offers a pine 'Swap' chip beside 'Remove'. Swapping means naming a replacement drug, which product rule 6 forbids outright ('AI must not invent medication substitutions') and which #51 already records as having no knowledge base behind it. The row ships with 'Remove', which is the action the safety model actually recognises as resolving the conflict, and it says Remove so the doctor is never told the app chose a replacement.
deviations.openQuestion: Same dependency as #51 — a substitution knowledge base with clinical sign-off.

deviations.summary: Conflicts are shown only where the SERVER flagged them, never computed on the client
deviations.reason: Frame 45 marks the offending medicine. The implementation renders exactly the warnings the safety layer returned, keyed to the drug they name. It does NOT match medicine names against the patient's allergies itself: doing so would mean asserting that amoxicillin is a penicillin — clinical class knowledge the app does not have (#51) — and product rule 7 forbids converting that uncertainty into clinical truth. A medicine typed by hand therefore carries no flag unless the server flagged it, which is honest about what the app actually knows.
deviations.ruling: Self-resolved: rules 6 and 7 already decide it; nothing new is being chosen.

deviations.summary: GOVERNANCE: standing authority to rule non-clinical product decisions, with a reversible log
deviations.reason:
2026-09-07 - OWNER RULING, verbatim: 'Decide non-clinical, log it.' Layout, copy, workflow and information-architecture decisions are the agent's to make during this migration rather than stalling it. Each such decision is recorded here as an APPROVED-DEVIATION carrying its reasoning, and the owner receives one review list at the end which they may reverse in whole or in part.

UNCHANGED AND STILL BLOCKING: clinical decisions, privacy/RBAC decisions, anything touching PHI, removal of existing functionality, and clinical hard-block policy. Those classify the frame BLOCKED and wait for the owner, exactly as before. Product rules 1-8 in CLAUDE.md are not re-litigable under this authority.
deviations.ownerRuling: Decide non-clinical, log it. Clinical, privacy/RBAC and PHI still block and wait.

deviations.summary: GATE C: a frame does not close until its screen actually works
deviations.reason: 2026-09-07 - OWNER DIRECTION, verbatim: 'in the end i want complete end to end working app.' Visual fidelity is necessary but not sufficient. On top of Gate A (nothing lost) and Gate B (matches the design), every frame must pass Gate C: the route is reachable through real navigation; every control on it is wired to a real endpoint or a real client action; the flow it belongs to can be completed end to end against the live API with seeded data; and there are no dead buttons, placeholder screens or TODO surfaces. A screen that photographs correctly but does nothing is NOT complete.

deviations.summary: The conflict line states the allergy and the class; it cannot state when it was recorded or the reaction
deviations.reason:
Frame 27's line reads 'Penicillin allergy — recorded 2019, reaction: rash'. The record stores an allergy as encrypted free text (Patient.allergiesEnc) plus a medicalFlags enum. There is no recorded-on date and no reaction field, so two thirds of that line has nothing behind it. Inventing them is exactly what product rule 7 forbids — turning uncertain information into clinical truth on screen.

So the line says what is actually known and why it matters: 'Allergy conflict: patient lists Penicillin. Amoxicillin is a penicillin. Verify before prescribing.' It is longer than the frame's and wraps to three lines rather than two. That cost is accepted: the frame's compactness comes from data the clinic never captured.

If the allergy model later gains a recorded-at and a reaction, this line should shorten to the frame's shape.

deviations.summary: The resolved warning lands in the SAFETY banner, not inline on a swapped row
deviations.reason:
Frame 28 shows the resolution on the row itself: 'Azithromycin 500 — swapped for Amoxicillin · allergy-safe [Undo]'. That shape depends on deviation #51 — a swap the app deliberately does not perform, because product rule 6 forbids the AI inventing a medication substitution.

Resolving by REMOVAL leaves no row for the resolved warning to sit on. Dropping it there would break the card's stated invariant that a resolved warning re-renders with a check and is never silently removed — 'I dealt with that' must not look like 'nothing was ever raised'. So partitionSafety() routes it to the standalone SAFETY block, struck through with a check.

The consequence visible in the capture: medicine count reads 'Medicines · 1' where the frame reads 2, because the conflicting drug is gone rather than replaced.

deviations.summary: NEXT SITTING shows the date; the frame also shows a time and the procedure
deviations.reason:
The frame reads 'Thu 16 Jul · 10:00 · obturation'. What the extraction produces is a follow-up INTERVAL ('review next week') — afterDays — not a booked slot. There is no time because nothing has been scheduled yet, and no procedure name because the next sitting's procedure is not dictated.

Printing a plausible 10:00 would be a fabricated appointment a receptionist could act on. The tile shows the date it can derive and stays a link to the real booking flow, where a time is chosen against actual availability.

deviations.summary: The card keeps an '+ Add medicine' affordance and a procedure sub-label the frames do not draw
deviations.reason:
Two additions the frames do not show, both retained under the Gate A rule that functionality is never removed for pixel fidelity:

1. '+ Add medicine' — the doctor must be able to add a drug the dictation missed. Without it the only route is re-recording the whole consultation.
2. The TOOTH tile carries the procedure ('RCT') beneath the number. The frame's tile shows the number alone; the tooth and what was done to it are read together everywhere else in this app.

Both are additive and neither displaces frame content.

deviations.summary: The prose region is empty, leaving vertical space the frames fill with FINDINGS and PROCEDURE
deviations.reason:
A visible consequence of ruling #52/#90 rather than a separate decision, recorded because it is what a reviewer sees first in the side-by-side: with no findings or procedure narrative extracted, the band between the medicine list and the CTA is blank, where the frames carry two paragraphs.

The sections are omitted rather than filled — PaperBlock renders what has data and never generates prose (product rule 7). The layout is not re-tuned to close the gap, because the gap is honest: it shows the record is thinner than the design assumed, and it will fill in on its own if the extraction fields are added later.

deviations.summary: GATE C FIX: the medicine row was a <button> containing the Remove and Undo buttons
deviations.reason:
Found while driving frame 28's capture. MedicineRow wrapped its whole body in a <button> whenever it had an onClick, so the conflict's 'Remove' chip and the resolved row's 'Undo' were buttons nested inside a button. React logged it on every render ('In HTML, %s cannot be a descendant of <%s>').

It was not only invalid. A button's accessible name is the concatenation of its contents, so the row announced itself as 'Amoxicillin 500mg TID 5 days Allergy conflict: patient lists Penicillin … Remove'. A screen-reader user could not distinguish the row from the action inside it — and the capture driver could not either: getByRole('button', { name: /remove/i }) matched the ROW and clicked that instead, which is how it surfaced.

The row is now a div with a stretched hit-area button behind content that ignores pointer events; the real actions opt back in above it. Pixel-identical, correctly nested, and the row carries an explicit name of its own.

deviations.summary: A voiced allergy lands inside 'More details' instead of a prominent chip
deviations.reason:
Frame 36 puts the allergy in the flags row as a red 'Allergy: Penicillin' chip, beside Diabetes/BP/Thyroid — visible without scrolling or expanding anything.

The implementation captures it correctly: extractPatientIntake parses 'allergic to penicillin', the form writes it to the ALLERGIES field, and setMoreOpen(true) auto-expands the section so it is not silently hidden. But that section sits below the fold, so the most safety-critical fact the intake captured is the least visible thing on the screen, while six medical-flag chips the patient does NOT have occupy the prominent row.

This is a MUST-FIX rather than a deviation because the frame and product rule 2 agree: doctor-facing clinical surfaces must surface allergies prominently, and /patients/new is doctor-only. Implementing the frame here IS implementing the rule; no product decision is needed.

Fix: render voiced allergies as crit-toned chips in the FLAGS row, keeping the free-text ALLERGIES field in More details as the editable source of truth. Owned by Task 20.
deviations.resolution: Fixed 2026-09-08: voiced allergies render as crit chips in the form body, above FLAGS. The free-text ALLERGIES field under More details stays the editable source of truth; the chip is a readout, so the two cannot drift.

deviations.summary: CHIEF COMPLAINT is a primary field in the frame and an expandable one in the app
deviations.reason:
Frame 36 shows CHIEF COMPLAINT as a first-class field between AGE & GENDER and MEDICAL FLAGS, filled and wearing the lime voice spine ('Pain on chewing, lower left'). The implementation puts it inside 'More details' alongside address and blood group.

The chief complaint is why the patient is here. It is the field the doctor reads first and the one the dictation is most likely to fill; grouping it with 'referred by' misreads its weight. Same root as #102 — the form's primary/secondary split does not match the frame's, and the frame's is right.

Owned by Task 20, which owns frames 35 and 36.
deviations.resolution: Fixed 2026-09-08: CHIEF COMPLAINT is a primary field between AGE/GENDER and the flags, as the frame has it.

deviations.summary: The patient code is generated and shown in the title, not as a short 'P-0413' chip
deviations.reason:
The frame shows a tidy 'P-0413' chip top-right and repeats it in the CTA ('Create patient · P-0413'). The app generates codes with a collision-resistant scheme and shows the real one — 'PT-PDFUHW' in this capture — in the header.

The frame's format implies a per-clinic sequential counter. That is a schema and concurrency decision (two receptionists creating patients at once must not both get P-0413), not a visual one, and the existing generator already solves it. Showing a prettier code than the record actually carries would mean the chip and the database disagree.

Recorded rather than matched. If sequential per-clinic codes are wanted, that is its own task with its own uniqueness story.

deviations.summary: The dictation card carries a full-width CTA where the frame has a mic circle
deviations.reason:
The frame's 'Say the details' card ends in a compact lime mic circle. The implementation renders a full-width 'Speak patient details' pill beneath the example line.

A bare mic circle reads as decoration next to an example sentence in quotes; in testing the labelled control is what makes it obvious the app is waiting to be spoken to, which is the whole premise of the product. The card is taller as a result and pushes the form down by roughly one field.

Kept deliberately. Decided under #94 as an interface decision, and reversible if the owner prefers the frame's restraint.

deviations.summary: AGE and GENDER keep their own labels where the frame uses one 'AGE & GENDER'
deviations.reason:
The frame labels the shared row once, 'AGE & GENDER'. The implementation keeps a label per field on the same row.

They are two separate inputs with separate validation and separate error slots — age can be invalid while gender is fine, and an error under a joint label cannot say which half it belongs to. The row grouping, which is what the frame is really doing, is matched.

deviations.summary: FLAGS is a full picker; the frame shows only the flags that are set plus a '+'
deviations.reason:
Frame 36 shows three chips — Diabetes, BP, Thyroid — and a '+' to add more. That is a SUMMARY of what is set on an existing record.

This screen is the opposite situation: a form being filled for the first time, where the receptionist has to find the right flag rather than review chosen ones. Showing all six as a multi-select makes the vocabulary discoverable; a '+' hides it behind a tap and a second surface. Voice-extracted flags outside the standard six still render as pre-selected custom chips, so nothing dictated is lost either way.

The frame's treatment is the better one on a record being reviewed, and the patient-detail surfaces use it there.

deviations.summary: A doctor's More hub shows three module tiles; the frame draws four, including Billing
deviations.reason:
Frame 70 shows Lab, Messages, Inventory and Billing. The capture is a DOCTOR session and shows three: `/billing` is RECEPTIONIST/ADMIN in lib/rbac.ts, so `canAccess('/billing', role)` hides the tile.

This is the rule working, not a missing tile. Rendering a route the role cannot open leaks the shape of the permission model and hands the user a tile that 403s. The frame depicts a reception or admin view, where all four appear.

The module grid reflows from four tiles to three; nothing else moves.

deviations.summary: Hub values are absent rather than zero while their query is loading or failed
deviations.reason:
Every chip on this hub — '1 doctor', '2 upcoming', '12', '1 request' — renders only when its query has answered with a non-zero value. A loading or failed query renders no chip at all.

The alternative is a chip that reads '0 doctors' for a moment and then corrects itself. A clinic always has at least one doctor, so zero is never a fact about the clinic; it is only ever a fact about the request, and printing it tells the reader something false about their own clinic.

So the frame's populated hub is what a loaded hub looks like, and an unloaded one is quieter than the frame rather than wrong.

generalRule: Functionality, security, RBAC, accessibility and legal requirements are never removed for pixel-level fidelity. Where a deviation is approved, preserve the functionality and reproduce the v9 visual language around it. No additional deviation is created without asking first.
rule: EVERY COMPLETED TASK LEAVES ZERO OPEN PRODUCT-DECISION ITEMS FOR THAT TASK. Open decisions are raised and resolved within the task that surfaced them. They are never carried forward: a pile of 20-30 unresolved deviations at the end is a pile nobody can remember the reason for.
